citation: Mayr, A., Klambauer, G., Unterthiner, T., Steijaert, M., Wegner, J. K., Ceulemans, H., Clevert, D.-A., & Hochreiter, S. (2016). Frontiers in Environmental Science, 3, 80.
title: DeepTox: Toxicity Prediction using Deep Learning
research_objective: Construct a high-performance deep learning pipeline predicting chemical toxicity across the 12 Tox21 assays for the Tox21 Data Challenge.
methodology_summary: Extracted massive static descriptors and circular fingerprints (ECFP); trained multi-task deep neural networks with masked loss functions across sparse label matrices; extracted hidden layer representations for downstream ensemble modeling.
key_findings: Deep neural networks with multi-task learning significantly outperformed single-task shallow models by transferring chemical representations across correlated biological pathways; hidden layer activations naturally learned known toxicophore substructures.
limitations: Representation sharing provides diminishing returns on assays with very few active compounds or unshared biological mechanisms.
pipeline_relevance: Direct foundation and justification for Member 2 multi-task deep neural network with masked loss and Member 3 hybrid architecture combining learned embeddings with descriptors.

citation: Wu, Z., Ramsundar, B., Feinberg, E. N., Gomes, J., Geniesse, C., Pappu, A. S., Leswing, K., & Pande, V. (2018). Chemical Science, 9(2), 513–530.
title: MoleculeNet: a benchmark for molecular machine learning
research_objective: Establish standardized datasets and rigorous molecular splitting methodologies to systematically benchmark molecular machine learning algorithms.
methodology_summary: Curated multiple chemical datasets (including Tox21); formalized the Bemis-Murcko scaffold split benchmark to test out-of-distribution chemical generalization against random splits.
key_findings: Random splits yield artificially high performance estimates because test compounds share identical core scaffolds with training data; scaffold splits expose realistic out-of-distribution generalization gaps.
limitations: Scaffold clustering can produce class distribution imbalances between partitions if active scaffolds are rare or concentrated in single chemical clusters.
pipeline_relevance: Justifies the Bemis-Murcko scaffold split requirement and provides standard baseline metrics to contextualize Member 4 scaffold vs. random split generalization penalties.

citation: Huang, R., Sakamuru, S., Martin, M. T., Reif, D. M., Judson, R. S., Houck, K. A., Casey, W., Hsieh, J.-H., Shockley, K. R., Ceger, P., Fostel, J., Witt, K. L., Tong, W., Rotroff, D. M., Zhao, T., Shinn, P., Simeonov, A., Dix, D. J., Austin, C. P., Kavlock, R. J., Tice, R. R., & Xia, M. (2014). Scientific Reports, 4, 5664.
title: Profiling of the Tox21 10K compound library for agonists and antagonists of the estrogen receptor alpha signaling pathway
research_objective: Profile the Tox21 10K chemical library using quantitative high-throughput screening (qHTS) to identify potential endocrine-disrupting chemicals and characterize assay specificity.
methodology_summary: Screened ~10,000 environmental chemicals across concentration-response curves using full-length receptor assays (NR-ER) and transfected ligand-binding domain assays (NR-ER-LBD).
key_findings: Full-length assays capture broader pathway activation while LBD assays provide higher target-specific binding fidelity; screening protocols naturally yield incomplete assay coverage across compounds due to multi-tiered screening rounds.
limitations: qHTS screening is subject to cell-based assay artifacts, compound autofluorescence interference, and cytotoxicity at high concentrations.
pipeline_relevance: Establishes primary biological provenance for the 12 endpoints; clarifies the mechanistic distinction between full receptor and LBD assays; explains why missing labels must be masked rather than assumed inactive.

citation: Fourches, D., Muratov, E., & Tropsha, A. (2010). Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling, 50(7), 1189–1204.
title: Trust, but Verify: On the Importance of Chemical Structure Curation in Cheminformatics and QSAR Modeling Research
venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
research_objective: Define a rigorous, standardized chemical structure curation workflow to sanitize molecular datasets prior to QSAR modeling and bioactivity prediction.
methodology_summary: Systematic pipeline for chemical structure validation: valence checking, stripping counterions and salts, normalizing tautomers, resolving organometallic bonding, and handling stereoisomeric duplicates with conflicting bioactivity.
key_findings: Demonstrated that undiscovered structure errors and uncurated duplicates drastically degrade predictive accuracy; proper sanitization and handling of stereoisomeric label contradictions is essential.
limitations: Strict valence filters can inadvertently exclude legitimate organometallic compounds or non-standard coordination complexes.
pipeline_relevance: Validates Member 1 chemical sanitization protocol excluding the 8 hypervalent aluminum compounds ([AlH3], valence 6) and governs handling of the 107 stereoisomer sets (31 with conflicting bioactivity).
